'''''Felicia aethiopica''''' is a low shrublet of up to about {{cvt|50|cm|ft|frac=3}} high that is assigned to the family [[Asteraceae]]. It has rigid, leathery, [[Glossary of leaf morphology#obovate|inverted egg-shaped]] leaves, with only the lowest pair set oppositely. It has flower heads with an involucre of about {{cvt|8|mm|frac=3}} in diameter with bracts that each contain three resin ducts, and have one whorl of twelve to fourteen ray florets with about 11 mm long and 1½ mm wide blue straps surrounding many yellow disc florets. The plant is called '''wild aster''' or '''dwarf Felicia''' in English, and '''wilde-aster''' or  '''bloublombossie''' in [[Afrikaans]]. Flowering occurs year-round. Wild aster can be found in the [[Western Cape|Western]] and [[Eastern Cape]] provinces of South Africa.<ref name=Grau73>{{cite journal|first= J.|last= Grau|year= 1973|title= Revision der Gattung Felicia (Asteraceae)|journal= Mitteilungen der Botanischer Staatssammlung München|volume= IX|pages= 503–510|url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/15019162#page/519/mode/1up|access-date= 2017-11-12}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI PlantZAfrica|title= Felicia aethiopica|author= Olivia Pekeur|url= https://pza.sanbi.org/felicia-aethiopica}}</ref><ref name=FK>{{cite web|website= Fernkloof Natrue Reserve|title= Felicia aethiopica subsp. aethiopica|url= http://fernkloof.org.za/index.php/all-plants/plant-families/item/felicia-aethiopica-subsp-aethiopica}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first= John|last= Manning|year= 2007|title= Filed Guide to Fynbos|publisher= Struik Nature|location= Cape Town}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Felicia aethiopica'' subsp. ''aethiopica'' is a low, up to {{cvt|50|cm|ft|frac=3}} high, branched shrublet. Its [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s are loosely hairy to glandular. The lower stems are covered by reddish [[Bark (botany)|bark]]. The rigidly leathery leaves mostly [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|set alternately along the stems]], only those at base are [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|oppositely set]] (rarely also higher on the shoot opposite), usually standing out at a straight angle, those lower on the stem even often weakly descending. The leaves are narrow to broadly elliptic to [[Glossary of leaf morphology#obovate|inverted egg-shaped]], {{cvt|5–20|mm|frac=5}} long and {{cvt|2–8|mm}} wide, with rolled down margins, hairless to strong bristly hairy and glandular, and anything intermediate.<ref name=Grau73 />

The [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|flower heads]] sit individually on the clearly distinguished [[Peduncle (botany)|inflorescence stalks]] that are mostly richly glandular near the top. The bracts surrounding the head that jointly form the [[Bract#Involucral bracts|involucre]] of up to {{cvt|8|mm|frac=3}} in diameter, are arranged in two whorls. The bracts of the inner whorl are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#oblanceolate|Inverted lance-shaped]], about {{cvt|5|mm}} long and {{cvt|1|mm}} wide, ribbed, and a little bristly. The outer bracts are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#lanceolate|lance-shaped]], about {{cvt|6|mm}} long and 1 mm wide, with three sunken resin ducts, and consistent with the [[indumentum]] of the leaves, variously bristly hairy or also glandular. About twelve to fourteen female [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|ray florets]] have a blue strap of ligula of about {{cvt|11|mm}} long and 1½ mm (0.06 in) wide, blue.  These surround many [[Plant reproductive morphology#Terminology|bisexual]], disc florets with a yellow [[Petal#Corolla)|corolla]] of about {{cvt|4|mm}} long. In the center of each corolla are five free filaments and five [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] merged into a tube, through which the [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] grows when the floret opens, hoovering up the [[pollen]] on its shaft. At the tip of both style branches is a triangular appendage. Around the base of the corolla is one whorl of vigorous, equally long, white, shortly toothed, but smooth at their base, largely persistent [[Pappus (botany)|pappus bristles]] of about {{cvt|4|mm}} long. The eventually black, dry, one-seeded, [[Dehiscence (botany)|indehiscent]] fruits called [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|cypselae]] are inverted egg-shaped to elliptic, about {{cvt|3|mm}} long and 1½ mm (0.06 in) wide, have a ridge along the outline, are hairless or rarely have a few bristles near the top, and a further smooth seedskin.<ref name=Grau73 />

''Felicia aethiopica'' subsp. ''ecklonis'' differs in having entirely hairy cypselae.<ref name=Grau73 />

== Differences with related species ==
''Felicia aethiopica'' is often confused with ''[[Felicia amoena]]'' and ''[[Felicia amelloides]]''. ''F. aethiopica'' is a woody shrublet with mostly only the lowest pair of leaves opposite and the remainder alternate, twelve to fourteen ray florets and also can be distinguished by the three resin ducts in the involucral bracts, that lack in both other species. ''F. amoena'' is a biennial or perennial plant with at least the lowest four to six leaves in pairs as well as those at each branching, and the remainder alternate and may have up to twenty five ray florets. ''F. amelloides'' is a mostly perennial plant with all its leaves in pairs and about twelve ray florets.<ref name=Grau73 />

== Taxonomy ==
The wild aster was first described in 1768 by [[Nicolaas Laurens Burman]], based on a specimen in the [[herbarium]] collection of his father, the Dutch botanist and physician [[Johannes Burman]], that had been collected at ''Caput Bonae Spei'', a term used for the southwest of the Cape Province. He named it ''Aster aethiopicus''. [[Henri Cassini]] in 1817 described ''Agathaea microphylla''. In 1822, [[Kurt Polycarp Joachim Sprengel]] described ''Cineraria trachyphylla''. In 1832, [[Christian Friedrich Lessing]] described ''Aster ecklonis''. He also described ''Aster capensis'', based on a herbarium sheet that contains one twig of ''Felicia aethiopica'' and two twigs of ''F. amelloides'', and this has since created much confusion. Cassini's taxon was reassigned to the genus ''Cineraria'' by [[Jens Vahl]], who created the combination ''C. microphylla'' in 1836. [[Carl Heinrich "Bipontinus" Schultz]] described a slightly different plant in 1843, calling it ''Agathaea kraussii'', but he demoted it a year later to ''Agathaea amelloides β kraussii''. In 1865, [[William Henry Harvey]], reassigned Schultz's taxon to ''Aster'', creating ''A. kraussii'', but he also described ''Aster aethiopicus'' var. ''glandulosus''. [[Harry Bolus|Bolus]] and [[Anthony Hurt Wolley-Dod]] assign the species to the genus ''Felicia'' in 1950, creating the combination ''Felicia aethiopica''. [[Jürke Grau]] in his 1973 ''[[Taxonomy (biology)#Monograph and taxonomic revision|Revision]] of the genus ''Felicia'' (Asteraceae)'', considered tall these names [[Synonymy (taxonomy)|synonymous]], except for ''Aster ecklonis'' <small>Less.</small>, that he considered a subspecies, calling it ''F. aethiopica'' subsp. ''ecklonis''. The species is considered to be part of the [[Section (botany)|section]] [[Felicia (plant)#Neodetris|Neodetris]].<ref name=Grau73 />

The species name Latin ''aethiopica'' is a [[Latin]] word meaning "relating to Ethiopia or Africa in general".<ref name=CB>{{cite web|website= CasaBio|title= Felicia aethiopica|url= https://casabio.org/taxa/felicia-aethiopica}}</ref>

== Distribution, habitat and ecology ==
''Felicia aethiopica'' subsp. ''aethiopica'' has the smaller distribution of the subspecies. It is restricted to the [[Cape Peninsula]], the [[Kogelberg]] area, the neighborhood of [[Hermanus]] and [[Gansbaai]], the [[De Hoop Nature Reserve|Potberg]] and near [[Swellendam]]. Subsp. ''ecklonis'' stretches from the [[Cedarberg]] in the north via the mountains near [[Porterville, Western Cape|Porterville]] to [[Riviersonderend]] and [[Witsand]] to [[KwaZulu-Natal|Natal]].<ref name=Grau73 /> It grows on sandy or rocky flats and slopes.<ref name=FK /><ref name=CB />

== Conservation ==
The continued survival of both subspecies of ''Felicia aethiopica'' is considered to be of [[Least-concern species|least concern]] because their populations are stable.<ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia aethiopica subsp. aethiopica|url= https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia aethiopica subsp. ecklonis|url= https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-3}}</ref>
